entry: Peninsular state in the [[Great Lakes]] region of the United States. With a population of 10.13 million and an area of 96,716 sq mi (250,490 km²), Michigan is the tenth-most populous state. Its capital is Lansing and its largest city is [[Detroit]]. The state consists of the Lower Peninsula and the heavily forested Upper Peninsula, separated by the Straits of Mackinac. Indigenous peoples such as the [[Ojibwe]] lived in the region for thousands of years. French explorers claimed the area for [[New France]] in the 17th century; it came under British control after the [[French and Indian War]] in 1762. Michigan was admitted as the 26th state on January 26, 1837. It is widely known as the center of the U.S. [[Automotive industry|automotive industry]].

English musician, songwriter and film producer, lead singer and founder member of the [[The Rolling Stones|Rolling Stones]]. Jagger co-wrote most of the band's songs with guitarist [[Keith Richards]], a partnership described as one of the most successful in rock music history. His career has spanned more than six decades. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1989 as a member of the Rolling Stones and was knighted in 2003 for services to popular music. He starred in the films *Performance* (1970) and *Ned Kelly* (1970). In the 2000s he co-founded the production company Jagged Films, which produced feature films beginning with the 2001 historical drama *Enigma*. He studied at the [[London School of Economics]] before abandoning his studies for the band.

Cartoon character and mascot of the [[The Walt Disney Company|Walt Disney Company]]. Created in 1928 by [[Walt Disney]] and Ub Iwerks, Mickey is an anthropomorphic mouse who typically wears red shorts, large shoes and white gloves. He was created as a replacement for Oswald the Lucky Rabbit, and made his public debut in the 1928 short *Steamboat Willie*. He went on to appear in over 130 films, mostly short films, and has also been featured in comic strips, comic books and television series such as *The Mickey Mouse Club* (1955–1996). Traditionally portrayed as a sympathetic underdog, he was rebranded over time from a cheeky rogue to a nice guy. Ten of his cartoons were nominated for the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film, and *Lend a Paw* won in 1941. In 1978 he became the first cartoon character to have a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]].

American actor, one of the last surviving stars of the silent-film era. In a career spanning nearly nine decades he appeared in more than 300 films. He began as a child in [[Vaudeville]] and played the title role in the Mickey McGuire series of short films. He played Andy Hardy in 16 films for [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]] in the 1930s and 1940s, and was the top box-office attraction from 1939 to 1941. He received [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations for *Babes in Arms* (1939) and *The Human Comedy*, and was awarded a special Academy Juvenile Award in 1939. Drafted during [[World War II]], he entertained troops on stage and radio. In 1982 he won a Golden Globe Award and an Emmy for the television movie *Bill*, and received an Academy Honorary Award.

American actor and former professional boxer, known for leading roles in drama, action and thriller films. Films in which he has appeared have grossed over $1.9 billion worldwide. His performance in the neo-noir *Body Heat* (1981) drew critical attention, and [[Roger Ebert]] called it his "breakthrough role". He won acclaim for *Diner* (1982) and was a leading man in the 1980s in films such as *Rumble Fish* and *Angel Heart*. In 1991 he left acting to pursue professional boxing, retiring in 1994. He returned to acting in supporting roles, and his comeback culminated in *The Wrestler* (2008), for which he won the Golden Globe Award and BAFTA Award for Best Actor and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Actor.

Suborder of [[Bat|bats]], Microchiroptera, within the order Chiroptera. Microbats are distinguished from [[Megabat|megabats]] by size, echolocation and other features. They are 4 to 16 cm (1.6–6.3 in) long. Most feed on insects, but some of the larger species hunt birds, lizards, frogs, smaller bats or [[Fish|fish]]. Only three species feed on the blood of large mammals or birds; these are the [[Vampire bat|vampire bats]] of South and Central America. Most leaf-nosed microbats eat fruit and nectar, though some hunt lizards and birds. Microbats have a tragus in the ear, thought crucial to echolocation. Molecular evidence suggests a different subdivision, because microbats have been shown to be paraphyletic.

Resting or dormant stage of a [[Microorganism|microorganism]], marked by suspended metabolism. Encystment, the process of cyst formation, can help a microbe disperse or survive unfavorable conditions such as lack of nutrients or oxygen, extreme temperatures, desiccation, adverse pH and toxic chemicals. Many groups of single-celled microbes possess this ability. Cysts can also be sites for nuclear reorganization and cell division. In parasitic species the cyst is often the infectious stage between hosts. When conditions become favorable, the cyst wall breaks down in a process called excystation. The idea that microbes could enter such a state was first described in 1702 by [[Antonie van Leeuwenhoek]], who studied rotifers. In 1872 Wilhelm Preyer introduced the term *anabiosis*, meaning return to life.

Scientific study of [[Microorganism|microorganisms]], which may be unicellular, multicellular or acellular. The field includes virology, bacteriology, [[Protist|protistology]], [[Mycology]], immunology and parasitology. Organisms are classified as prokaryotes or eukaryotes. Microbiologists traditionally relied on culture, staining and microscopy, but less than 1% of the microorganisms in common environments can be cultured in isolation with current means. Molecular tools, such as DNA sequence-based identification of the 16S rRNA gene for bacteria, are now central. The existence of microorganisms was predicted centuries before their discovery, for example by the Jains of India and by the Roman Marcus Terentius Varro. In 1666 [[Robert Hooke]] recorded the first microscope observation, of the fruiting bodies of moulds. [[Antonie van Leeuwenhoek]] observed microscopic organisms in the 1670s. Scientific microbiology developed in the 19th century through [[Louis Pasteur]], and medical microbiology through [[Robert Koch]].

Subregion of [[Oceania]] with approximately 2,000 small islands in the northwestern [[Pacific Ocean]]. The four main archipelagos are the Caroline, Gilbert, Mariana and Marshall islands. Political control is distributed among several sovereign nations, including [[Palau]], the [[Federated States of Micronesia]], [[Kiribati]] and [[Nauru]]. The Mariana Islands are affiliated with the United States, including [[Guam]] and the Northern Mariana Islands. The climate is tropical marine. Austronesian peoples settled the region after a seaborne expansion from Formosa around 3000 to 1500 BC. The first recorded European contact was in 1521, when the [[Magellan expedition]] landed in the Marianas. Jules Dumont d'Urville is usually credited with coining the term Micronesia in 1832, though Louis Domeny de Rienzi used it a year earlier.

Microscopic organism, either single-celled or a colony of cells; also called a microbe. Microorganisms are extremely diverse and represent most unicellular organisms in all three domains of life. [[Archaea]] and [[Bacteria]] contain only microorganisms, while the domain Eukaryota includes many unicellular protists and protozoans. They live from the poles to the equator, in deserts, geysers, rocks and the deep sea. Some are adapted to extreme heat, cold, pressure or radiation; *Deinococcus radiodurans* tolerates high radiation. Microbes are a vital component of fertile soil and make up the human microbiota, including the gut flora. Many infectious diseases are caused by microbes. Study began in the 1670s, when [[Antonie van Leeuwenhoek]] observed microorganisms under the microscope. In the 1850s [[Louis Pasteur]] found that they caused food spoilage, and in the 1880s [[Robert Koch]] showed that they caused [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]], [[Cholera]], diphtheria and [[Anthrax]].

Transducer for converting sound into an electrical signal. Microphones are used in telecommunication, sound recording, [[Broadcasting|broadcasting]] and [[Consumer electronics|consumer electronics]], including telephones, hearing aids and mobile devices. The most common types are the dynamic microphone, which uses a coil of wire suspended in a magnetic field; the condenser microphone, which uses the vibrating diaphragm as a capacitor plate; and the contact microphone, which uses a crystal of [[Piezoelectricity|piezoelectric]] material. Microphones usually need a preamplifier. The earliest devices to amplify the voice were acoustic megaphones, including Greek theater masks from the 5th century BC. Between 1664 and 1685 [[Robert Hooke]] experimented with an early telephone of stretched wire. The carbon microphone, which made proper voice telephony possible, was developed independently by David Hughes, [[Emile Berliner]] and [[Thomas Edison]]. In 1916 E.C. Wente of Western Electric developed the first condenser microphone.

American multinational technology conglomerate, headquartered in Redmond, Washington. Founded in 1975 by [[Bill Gates]] and [[Paul Allen]] to market BASIC interpreters for the Altair 8800, the company rose to dominate the PC operating system market with [[MS-DOS]] in the mid-1980s, followed by Windows. Its 1986 initial public offering created three billionaires. [[Steve Ballmer]] succeeded Gates as CEO in 2000, and Satya Nadella became CEO in 2014, shifting focus toward cloud computing. Microsoft is the largest software company by revenue. Its best-known products are the Windows operating systems and [[Microsoft Office]]; its hardware includes the Surface PCs and the [[Xbox]] consoles. Critics have cited monopolistic practices and software problems with ease of use, robustness and security. It has also been criticized for providing services to Israel during the [[Gaza war]].

Web search engine owned and operated by [[Microsoft]]. Developed by Microsoft AI, Bing traces its roots to MSN Search, Windows Live Search and Live Search. Microsoft CEO [[Steve Ballmer]] announced the transition from Live Search to Bing on May 28, 2009, and the official release followed on June 3, 2009. Under a deal with [[Yahoo|Yahoo!]], Bing powered Yahoo! Search. In February 2023 Microsoft launched Bing Chat, an AI chatbot based on GPT-4, later renamed Microsoft Copilot. As of April 2024, Bing held a 3.64% share of the global search market, second to Google's 90.91%.

[[Spreadsheet|Spreadsheet editor]] developed by [[Microsoft]] for Windows, macOS, Android, iOS and iPadOS. Excel offers calculation, graphing tools, pivot tables and a macro programming language, Visual Basic for Applications (VBA). It is used for [[Data analysis|data analysis]], and has been developed since 1985. It forms part of Microsoft 365 and [[Microsoft Office]]. Excel 2016 had 484 functions, classified into 14 categories. With the introduction of LAMBDA on December 3, 2020, Excel became Turing complete.

Office suite of productivity software developed by [[Microsoft]]. The first version, announced by [[Bill Gates]] on August 1, 1988, contained [[Microsoft Word]], [[Microsoft Excel]] and [[Microsoft PowerPoint]]. The suite now includes OneNote and Outlook, and the Windows version also includes the Access database program. Since Office 2013 Microsoft has promoted subscription-based Microsoft 365, formerly Office 365, as the primary means of obtaining the suite. Revenue from Office 365 overtook conventional license sales in 2017. Microsoft still sells the perpetually licensed suite, the latest version of which is Office 2024.

Personal information manager and [[Email|email]] client from [[Microsoft]], available as part of the Microsoft 365 suite. Primarily popular with businesses, Outlook also provides calendaring, task and contact management, note-taking, journal logging and RSS news aggregation. Organizations can deploy it as multi-user software through Microsoft Exchange Server or SharePoint, for shared mailboxes, calendars and folders. Outlook replaced Microsoft's earlier Schedule+ and Exchange Client. Microsoft Entourage served Macintosh users until Outlook for Mac 2011, the first native version of Outlook for Mac OS X. Privacy concerns have been raised about the new Outlook, which sends passwords, mail and other data to Microsoft.

Presentation program developed by [[Microsoft]] and part of [[Microsoft Office]]. It was created by Robert Gaskins and Dennis Austin at Forethought, Inc., and released on April 20, 1987, initially for Macintosh computers. Microsoft acquired it for about $14 million three months later, its first significant acquisition. PowerPoint became part of Microsoft Office in 1989 for Macintosh and in 1990 for Windows. Since the late 1990s its share of presentation software has been estimated at 95 percent. The third version (1992) introduced video output of virtual slideshows to digital projectors, which over time replaced physical transparencies and slides. Its wide use in business has drawn strong reactions, including advice that presentations should be used less, differently or better.

Family of proprietary operating systems developed by [[Microsoft]]. The first version, Windows 1.0, was released on November 20, 1985, as a graphical shell for [[MS-DOS]]. The name refers to the windowing system of graphical user interfaces. The 1990 release of Windows 3.0 brought market success. All members of the family are based on the [[Windows NT]] line, whose first version, Windows NT 3.1, was intended for servers and corporate workstations. Windows is the most popular desktop operating system, with a 77% market share as of October 2026, and the second-most popular operating system overall, behind [[Android (operating system)|Android]]. Windows 11 is the most used desktop version, with a 74% share.

[[Word processor|Word processing program]] developed by [[Microsoft]]. It was first released on October 25, 1983, as Multi-Tool Word for Xenix systems, and later ran on DOS, the Classic Mac OS, Windows (1989), macOS, iOS and Android. Unlike most MS-DOS programs of its time, it was designed for use with a mouse and offered WYSIWYG display. Word for Mac, released in 1985, was the first graphical version. It became the de facto standard word processor from the 1990s, when it eclipsed WordPerfect. Word is sold as a standalone product or as part of [[Microsoft Office]], under a perpetual license or Microsoft 365 subscription.

Form of [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]] with wavelengths of about 1 m to 1 mm, between radio waves and infrared light. Microwaves correspond to frequencies between 300 MHz and 300 GHz, though definitions vary. Frequencies in the microwave range are often referred to by IEEE radar band designations such as S, C, X, Ku, K and Ka. Microwaves travel by line-of-sight, so terrestrial microwave links are limited by the visual horizon to about 40 miles (64 km). They are used in [[Radar|radar]], satellite and spacecraft communication, [[Telecommunications|telecommunications]] and wireless networks, remote sensing, [[Spectroscopy|spectroscopy]], particle accelerators, medical diathermy and cancer treatment, and in [[Microwave oven|microwave ovens]]. Radio astronomy uses microwaves to detect the [[Cosmic microwave background]].

Electric kitchen appliance for heating and cooking food with [[Microwave|microwave]] radiation. Microwaves cause polar molecules in food to rotate and generate heat, a process known as dielectric heating. Heating is fairly uniform in the outer 25–38 mm (1–1.5 inches) of a homogeneous, high-water-content food. The development of the [[Cavity magnetron|cavity magnetron]] in the United Kingdom made it practical to heat water molecules efficiently. American engineer Percy Spencer is generally credited with the first commercial model, the Raytheon Radarange, sold in 1947, which was based on British [[Radar]] technology developed before and during [[World War II]]. Sharp introduced the first model with a turntable between 1964 and 1966, and Amana introduced a countertop model in 1967. Microwave ovens usually do not brown food, because they rarely reach the temperatures needed for [[Maillard reaction|Maillard reactions]].

[[Mid-ocean ridge]] along the floor of the [[Atlantic Ocean]], a divergent tectonic plate boundary. The ridge is part of the longest mountain range in the world. It separates North America from Eurasia and Africa north of the [[Azores]], and separates Africa from South America to the south. It runs from near Greenland to [[Bouvet Island]]. Mostly underwater, it rises above sea level in [[Iceland]]. The ridge spreads at an average rate of about 2.5 cm (1 in) per year. Matthew Fontaine Maury first inferred it in 1853. Research on the global ridge system supported [[Alfred Wegener]]'s theory of continental drift, which led to seafloor spreading and [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]]. A deep rift valley runs along its axis, where magma erupts as lava to form new crust. Near the equator the Romanche Trench divides the ridge into North and South Atlantic ridges.

Underwater mountain system formed by [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonic]] spreading. A mid-ocean ridge is where seafloor spreading occurs at a divergent plate boundary. Mantle material rises as [[Magma|magma]] at the linear weakness between separating plates and emerges as [[Lava|lava]], creating new oceanic crust and [[Lithosphere|lithosphere]] on cooling. A ridge typically lies at a depth of about 2,600 meters (8,500 ft) and rises about 2,000 meters (6,600 ft) above the deepest part of an ocean basin. The first one discovered, the [[Mid-Atlantic Ridge]], gave the name. Linked together, mid-ocean ridges form a global system that is the longest mountain range in the world, 65,000 km (40,400 mi) long. Spreading rates range from approximately 10–200 mm/yr. [[Hydrothermal vent|Hydrothermal vents]] along the ridges support ecosystems that do not depend on sunlight.

[[Benzodiazepine]] medication, sold as Versed among others, for [[Anesthesia|anesthesia]] and procedural sedation. It induces sleepiness, reduces anxiety and causes anterograde amnesia, but does not render a person unconscious. It is also used to treat prolonged seizures and severe agitation. It can be given by mouth, intravenously, into a muscle, into the nose or through the cheek. Side effects can include slowed breathing, low blood pressure and sleepiness. It was patented in 1974 and came into medical use in 1982. It is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines.

entry: Theater of [[World War I]], 1914–18, between the [[Ottoman Empire]] and Allied powers. Ottoman forces, aided by many Kurdish tribes, Circassians and [[Arabs]], fought with some help from the [[Central Powers]]. British, Dominion, Russian, French and Indian troops fought for the Allies. The four main campaigns were the Sinai and Palestine, Mesopotamian, [[Caucasus]] and [[Gallipoli campaign|Gallipoli]] campaigns. Four minor campaigns were fought in Iran, South Arabia, the Arabian interior and Libya. Arab forces joined the Allies in the Arab Revolt, proclaimed by Sharif Hussein of [[Mecca]] in June 1916. Russian participation ended with the Armistice of Erzincan on December 5, 1917. The Ottomans accepted the Armistice of Mudros on October 30, 1918, and later signed the Treaty of Sèvres (August 10, 1920) and the Treaty of Lausanne (July 24, 1923).
